body:
Slow sand filtration treats drinking water through two processes working together: biological degradation and physical filtration. The source describes water passing first through a living layer, then through fine sand and gravel below it.

The living layer is a biofilm known as the schmutzdecke. It develops on the top 1 to 2 centimeters of the fine sand, and the microorganisms in it actively feed on pathogens, bacteria and organic particles carried in by the water. This thin film is the biological part of the filter.

Below the schmutzdecke, the mechanical part takes over. Water moves down through the sand and then the gravel, and straining through these layers removes the suspended particulates that remain.

Speed is the key operating limit. The source gives typical filtration rates of 0.1 to 0.2 meters per hour, and says the rate must stay low to avoid disrupting the active biofilm. Pushing water through faster risks damaging the very layer that does the biological work.

Know the limits of this description. The source excerpt covers pathogens, bacteria, organic particles and suspended particulates. It says nothing about dissolved chemical pollutants such as pesticides, fuels or heavy metals, so do not treat a slow sand filter as a chemical treatment. It is also a summary of principles, not a construction or testing guide.

review.scope: Source consistency check: verifies that the statements about the schmutzdecke biofilm, mechanical straining through sand and gravel, and the 0.1 to 0.2 meters per hour filtration rate directly reflect the provided source excerpt, that attribution is accurate, and that the missing coverage of chemical pollutants is declared as a limitation. Not independent laboratory or scientific verification.

sources.title: EPA — Slow Sand Filtration for Small Water Systems

summary: Slow sand filtration pairs a living biofilm, the schmutzdecke, on the top 1 to 2 cm of fine sand with mechanical straining through sand and gravel. The flow must stay low, typically 0.1 to 0.2 meters per hour, to protect the biofilm.
title: Let a living layer filter the water slowly
